title: Properties of Metals
quiz_topic: Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress

objectives.text: Without references, DESCRIBE how changes in stress, strain, and physical and chemical properties effect the materials used in a reactor plant.

passages.quote: Stress is the internal resistance of a material to the distorting effects of an external force or load.
Tensile stress is that type of stress in which the two sections of material on either side of a stress plane tend to pull apart or elongate as illustrated in Figure 1(a).
Compressive stress is the reverse of tensile stress.
Shear stress exists when two parts of a material tend to slide across each other in any typical plane of shear upon application of force parallel to that plane as illustrated in Figure 1(c).
The plane of a shear stress lies in the plane of the force system from which it originates.
The ability of a material to react to compressive stress or pressure is called compressibility.

There are many types of stresses, but they can all be generally classified in one of six categories: residual stresses, structural stresses, pressure stresses, flow stresses, thermal stresses, and fatigue stresses.
Strain is the proportional dimensional change, or the intensity or degree of distortion, in a material under stress.
Strain may take two forms; elastic strain and plastic deformation.
Elastic strain is a transitory dimensional change that exists only while the initiating stress is applied and disappears immediately upon removal of the stress.
Plastic deformation (or plastic strain) is a dimensional change that does not disappear when the initiating stress is removed.
The state of stress just before plastic strain begins to appear is known as the proportional limit, or elastic limit, and is defined by the stress level and the corresponding value of elastic strain.
A face-centered cubic crystal structure will deform more readily under load before breaking than a body-centered cubic structure.
Hooke's Law states that in the elastic range of a material strain is proportional to stress.
Young's Modulus (Elastic Modulus) is the ratio of stress to strain, or the gradient of the stress-strain graph.
The elongation of the bar is directly proportional to the tensile force and the length of the bar and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area and the modulus of elasticity.
The Bulk Modulus of Elasticity is the elastic response to hydrostatic pressure and equilateral tension or the volumetric response to hydrostatic pressure and equilateral tension.
Fracture point is the point where the material fractures due to plastic deformation.
Hooke's Law applies between Points 1 and 2.
Elastic region is between Points 1 and 2.
Plastic region is between Points 2 and 5.
Ductile material will deform (elongate) more than brittle material, shown in the figures within the text.
Strength is the ability of a material to resist deformation.
Decreasing the grain size through cold or hot working of the metal tends to retard slip and thus increases the strength of the metal.
An increase in slip will decrease the strength of a material.
Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) is the maximum resistance to fracture.
the ultimate tensile strength appears as the stress coordinate value of the highest point on the curve.
Yield strength is the stress at which a predetermined amount of permanent deformation occurs.
Ductility is the ability of a material to deform easily upon the application of a tensile force, or the ability of a material to withstand plastic deformation without rupture.
An increase in temperature will increase ductility.
Ductility decreases with lower temperatures, cold working, and irradiation.
Ductility is desirable in high temperature and high pressure applications.
Malleability is the ability of a metal to exhibit large deformation or plastic response when being subjected to compressive force.
Toughness describes how a material reacts under sudden impacts.
It is defined as the work required to deform one cubic inch of metal until it fractures.
Hardness is the property of a material that enables it to resist plastic deformation, penetration, indentation, and scratching.
Hardness and tensile strength increase in heat-treated steel; toughness and ductility decrease.
Generally, the faster a metal is cooled, the smaller the grain sizes will be.
Welding can induce internal stresses that will remain in the material after the welding is completed.
This elongation of the material causes residual compressive and tensile stresses in the material.
Welding stresses can be minimized by using heat sink welding, which results in lower metal temperatures, and by annealing.
Corrosion is the deterioration of a material due to interaction with its environment.
Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals with different potentials are placed in electrical contact in an electrolyte.
Galvanic corrosion is of particular concern in design and material selection.
Material selection is important because different metals come into contact with each other and may form galvanic cells.
Design is important to minimize differing flow conditions and resultant areas of corrosion buildup.
The less resistant, more active one becomes the anodic (negative) corrosion site.

Hydrogen embrittlement is the process by which steel loses its ductility and strength due to tiny cracks that result from the internal pressure of hydrogen (H2) or methane gas (CH4), which forms at the grain boundaries.
The conditions required for hydrogen embrittlement in steel is the presence of hydrogen dissolved in the water and the carbon in the steel.
The methane gas collects in small voids along the grain boundaries where it builds up enormous pressures that initiate cracks and decrease the ductility of the steel.
Hydrogen embrittlement is not a permanent condition.
Zircaloy-4 is less susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement than zircaloy-2 because:
Studies at Westinghouse, Batelle, and elsewhere have revealed that the nickel in the zircaloy-2 was responsible for the hydrogen pickup.

body.text: Stress: σ = F/A, where F is the applied force and A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force.

body.alt: Three bars: forces pulling apart across a stress plane for tensile, pressing together for compressive, and sliding along the plane for shear.

body.text: In compressive stress, adjacent parts of the material tend to press against each other through a stress plane.
The plane of a tensile or compressive stress lies perpendicular to the axis of the force.

checks.q: In which stress do two parts of a material tend to slide across each other?
checks.x: Shear stress exists when two parts of a material tend to slide across each other upon application of force parallel to that plane.

checks.q: How is the plane of a shear stress oriented?
o: In the plane of the force system
checks.x: The plane of a shear stress lies in the plane of the force system from which it originates.

checks.q: A force of 1,000 lbf acts on a cross-sectional area of 2 in.². What is the stress?
checks.x: Stress is force divided by cross-sectional area: 1,000 lbf divided by 2 in.² is 500 psi.

body.text: Strain: ε = δ/L, where δ is the total elongation and L is the original length.
With elastic strain, the atoms all return to their original positions when the stress is removed, and no permanent deformation occurs.
Beyond the proportional limit, the deformation consists of both elastic and plastic strains.

body.cap: Change of Shape of Cylinder Under Stress
body.alt: A cylinder under tension gets longer and narrower. Under compression it gets shorter and wider.

body.text: When metal experiences strain, its volume remains constant, so if one dimension increases, another must decrease. There are a few exceptions, such as strain hardening.
Lattices with closely packed planes allow more plastic deformation, and cubic lattices allow slippage more easily than non-cubic lattices.
The BCC lattice, as in α-iron, is cubic but not closely packed and forms strong metals. The FCC lattice, as in γ-iron, is cubic and closely packed and forms more ductile materials.

checks.q: What happens to elastic strain when the stress is removed?
o: It remains as a permanent change
checks.x: Elastic strain exists only while the initiating stress is applied and disappears immediately upon removal of the stress.

checks.q: What are the two common forms of strain?
checks.x: Strain may take two forms: elastic strain and plastic deformation.

checks.q: Which iron lattice deforms more readily under load before breaking?
checks.x: A face-centered cubic crystal structure will deform more readily under load before breaking than a body-centered cubic structure.

checks.q: What is the proportional limit?
o: The highest point on the stress-strain curve
The stress when elastic strain disappears
The stress just before plastic strain begins to appear
checks.x: The state of stress just before plastic strain begins to appear is known as the proportional limit, or elastic limit.

body.text: δ = PL/AE, where P is the force, L the length of the bar, A the cross-sectional area, and E the Modulus of Elasticity.
E = σ/ε
Young's Modulus is measured in the same units as stress, pounds per square inch, because strain is a ratio of two lengths.

checks.q: A carbon steel bar 100 in. long with a 1 in.² area carries a 30,000 lb load. E is 3.0 x 10⁷ psi. What is the elongation?
What is Young's Modulus?
o: The ratio of strain to stress
The stress at which yielding begins
The ratio of stress to strain
checks.x: Young's Modulus (Elastic Modulus) is the ratio of stress to strain, or the gradient of the stress-strain graph.

checks.q: If the length of a bar under a set load is doubled, what happens to its elongation?
checks.x: The elongation of the bar is directly proportional to the tensile force and the length of the bar.

body.text: A tensile test applies a gradually increasing tension force to a sample until it is pulled apart, measuring load and elongation.

body.alt: Stress against elongation for a ductile material: a straight rise from Point 1 to proportional limit 2, yield point 3, a long curve up to ultimate tensile strength 4, and fracture point 5.

items: Point 2: proportional limit (PL) or elastic limit
Point 3: yield strength (YS) or yield point
Point 5: fracture point, at which failure occurs

body.text: If stress is removed in the elastic region, the material returns to its original length. In the plastic region, it does not.

body.alt: Stress against elongation for a brittle material: a steep rise with fracture at low elongation, and a short plastic region.

body.text: Figure 3 is typical of a ductile material, where the plastic region is great and the material will bear more strain before fracture. Figure 4 is typical of a brittle material, where the plastic region is small.

checks.q: On a stress-strain curve, what is the highest point?
checks.x: If the complete curve is available, the ultimate tensile strength appears as the stress coordinate of the highest point.

checks.q: A stress-strain curve has a large plastic region. What type of material does it show?
checks.x: Figure 3 is typical of a ductile material, where the plastic region is great. Ductile material will deform more than brittle material.

checks.q: Between which points of the stress-strain curve does Hooke's Law apply?
checks.x: Hooke's Law applies between Points 1 and 2, the elastic region.

checks.q: Which part of the stress-strain curve is the plastic region?
checks.x: Plastic region is between Points 2 and 5.

checks.q: What is the fracture point?
o: The point where the curve stops being straight
The point where the material fractures due to plastic deformation
The point where plastic strain begins
The highest stress on the curve
checks.x: Fracture point is the point where the material fractures due to plastic deformation.

body.text: The strength of a material is the maximum nominal stress it can sustain, and is always qualified by the type of stress, such as tensile, compressive, or shear strength.
UTS equals the maximum load divided by the area of the original cross section.
When a force is applied, layers of atoms move in relation to adjacent layers, which is slip. Grain boundaries tend to prevent slip, and smaller grains give a larger grain boundary area.

checks.q: How does an increase in slip affect a metal?
o: It has no effect on strength
checks.x: An increase in slip will decrease the strength of a material.

checks.q: Why does decreasing grain size increase the strength of a metal?
checks.x: Decreasing the grain size through cold or hot working of the metal tends to retard slip and thus increases the strength.

checks.q: What is strength?
o: The ability of a material to resist deformation
The ability to deform without rupture
The work to fracture a cubic inch of metal
checks.x: Strength is the ability of a material to resist deformation.

body.alt: A marked gage length before a test, a fracture through a neck, and the broken parts fitted together to find the final gage length.

body.text: Percent elongation and reduction of area are both indicators of ductility. Reduction of area is the better indicator, because it is measured at the minimum diameter of the neck.

A decrease in temperature causes a change from ductile to brittle behavior. Heating a cold-worked metal to or above the temperature at which its atoms return to their equilibrium positions increases ductility, and this is called annealing.
High ductility in these applications helps prevent brittle fracture.

checks.q: For which reactor plant applications is high ductility desirable?
o: High temperature and high pressure applications
Low temperature, low pressure piping only
checks.x: Ductility is desirable in high temperature and high pressure applications.

checks.q: What effect does an increase in temperature have on ductility?
checks.x: An increase in temperature will increase ductility.

body.alt: A cylinder squeezed axially bulges outward, with arrows showing surface and internal tension.

body.text: Toughness is measured by the Charpy test or the Izod test, which use a notched sample and a swinging pendulum.

body.alt: Pendulum impact tester with a meter, showing the notched specimen and the swing path.

body.text: The more energy the specimen absorbs, the smaller the upward swing of the pendulum and the tougher the material.
Resistance to wear by friction or erosion generally increases with hardness.

In concentrations of less than 5%, nickel raises the toughness and ductility of steel without raising the hardness. Chromium forms a carbide that hardens the metal. Stainless steels are alloy steels containing at least 12% chromium.

checks.q: Which property describes how a material reacts under sudden impacts?
checks.x: Toughness describes how a material reacts under sudden impacts.

checks.q: What does hardness enable a material to resist?
o: Plastic deformation, penetration, indentation, and scratching
checks.x: Hardness is the property of a material that enables it to resist plastic deformation, penetration, indentation, and scratching.

checks.q: What is malleability?
o: Large deformation or plastic response under compressive force
Easy deformation under a tensile force
checks.x: Malleability is the ability of a metal to exhibit large deformation or plastic response when being subjected to compressive force.

body.text: During manufacture, varying the rate of cooling (quenching) controls grain size and grain patterns, to produce different levels of hardness and tensile strength.
This makes the metal harder.
Annealing heats a component slowly to an elevated temperature, holds it there for a long time, then cools it.

items: Softens the steel and improves ductility
Relieves internal stresses from previous processes

body.text: Cold work is plastic deformation carried out so that strain hardening is not relieved, and it decreases ductility. Hot working deforms metals above their recrystallization temperature, and strain hardening does not occur.

checks.q: What happens to grain size as a metal is cooled faster?
checks.x: Generally, the faster a metal is cooled, the smaller the grain sizes will be.

body.text: In stainless steels such as type 304, the lattice is FCC (austenite). During high temperature welding, surrounding metal may reach 500°F to 1000°F, where austenite transforms to a BCC structure (bainite).
The bainite occupies more space than the original austenite lattice.

checks.q: What types of stress does welding leave in stainless steel?
checks.x: The elongation of the material causes residual compressive and tensile stresses in the material.

body.text: All metals and alloys are subject to corrosion. It cannot be eliminated, but it can be controlled.

A difference in electrical potential drives current through the electrolyte, and this current corrodes one of the metals. The larger the potential difference, the greater the probability of galvanic corrosion.
The stronger, more noble metal is cathodic and protected.
Loose corrosion products are important because they can be transported to the reactor core and irradiated.

checks.q: Why is galvanic corrosion a concern in material selection?
o: Different metals in contact may form galvanic cells
It only occurs in pure metals
checks.x: Material selection is important because different metals come into contact with each other and may form galvanic cells.

checks.q: In galvanic corrosion, which metal corrodes?
o: The less resistant, more active one
checks.x: The less resistant, more active one becomes the anodic (negative) corrosion site.

body.text: Hydrogen diffuses along the grain boundaries and combines with the carbon in the steel to form methane gas, which is not mobile.

body.alt: Hydrogen from a corrosive solution enters the metal, forms CH4 at grain boundaries, and opens a crack.

body.text: If the metal is under a high tensile stress, brittle failure can occur.
If cracking does not occur and no more hydrogen is generated at the surface, the hydrogen can rediffuse from the steel, so that ductility is restored.

checks.q: What two conditions are required for hydrogen embrittlement in steel?
o: Tensile stress and a low pH
Hydrogen dissolved in the water and carbon in the steel
Nickel in the steel and oxygen in the water
checks.x: The conditions required for hydrogen embrittlement in steel is the presence of hydrogen dissolved in the water and the carbon in the steel.

checks.q: Is hydrogen embrittlement of steel a permanent condition?
o: No, because it stops at room temperature
No, ductility can be restored if the hydrogen rediffuses
checks.x: Hydrogen embrittlement is not a permanent condition. If cracking does not occur, the hydrogen can rediffuse from the steel.

body.text: Zirconium reacts with water, and part of the hydrogen produced combines with the zirconium to form zirconium hydride platelets. The metal then becomes embrittled, and cracks begin in the platelets.

items: The introduction of niobium into zircaloy-4 reduces the amount of hydrogen absorption in the metal

checks.q: Why is zircaloy-4 less susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement than zircaloy-2?
o: It has a larger grain size
It contains less nickel, and niobium reduces hydrogen absorption
checks.x: Zircaloy-4 contains less nickel, and the introduction of niobium reduces the amount of hydrogen absorption in the metal.

examples.problem: What is the elongation of 200 in. of aluminum wire with a 0.01 square in. area if it supports a weight of 100 lb?

facts.q: What is the formula for stress?
facts.a: Stress equals force divided by cross-sectional area: σ = F/A.

facts.q: What are the six categories of stress?
facts.a: Residual, structural, pressure, flow, thermal, and fatigue stresses.
A transitory dimensional change that exists only while the initiating stress is applied.
The ratio of stress to strain, or the gradient of the stress-strain graph.
The ability of a material to deform easily upon the application of a tensile force, or to withstand plastic deformation without rupture.
How a material reacts under sudden impacts, defined as the work required to deform one cubic inch of metal until it fractures.
Corrosion that occurs when two dissimilar metals with different potentials are in electrical contact in an electrolyte.

facts.q: What is hydrogen embrittlement of steel?
facts.a: Loss of ductility and strength from tiny cracks caused by the internal pressure of hydrogen or methane gas at the grain boundaries.

summary.text: Stress is the internal resistance of a material to the distorting effects of an external force or load, and its three types are tensile, compressive, and shear.
Strain takes two forms: elastic strain, which disappears when the stress is removed, and plastic deformation, which does not.
Hooke's Law states that in the elastic range of a material strain is proportional to stress.
Hooke's Law applies between Points 1 and 2 of the stress-strain curve, and the plastic region is between Points 2 and 5.
Ductility decreases with lower temperatures, cold working, and irradiation.
Hardness and tensile strength increase in heat-treated steel, while toughness and ductility decrease.
Welding produces compressive and tensile stresses, which are minimized by heat sink welding and annealing.
Galvanic corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals exist at different electrical potentials in the presence of an electrolyte.
Zircaloy-4 is less susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement than zircaloy-2 because it contains less nickel and has niobium added.

blend_notes.note: The two hydrogen embrittlement pages are tagged Water-system only: the handbook's required condition is hydrogen dissolved in water, and zirconium hydriding starts with the zirconium-water reaction. Coolant pH and coolant hydrogen addition on p.37 are left off.

Galvanic corrosion stays untagged, as in CH-02. General corrosion in water, SCC, chloride stress corrosion, and inconel problems on p.32 to p.35 have no objective here, are taught in CH-02, and are left off.
p.23 on PWR components and the ASME code, and p.29 on the type 304 tritium reactor tank, are left off.
p.1 says that if the distortion disappears and the metal remains distorted, the strain is plastic, which contradicts itself. The lesson uses p.8.
p.2 gives the units of applied force as lbs of force per in.². The lesson does not repeat the unit.
p.8 treats proportional limit and elastic limit as one term, and p.23 describes them separately. The lesson uses p.8, which is the objective's source.
Figure 5 repeats Figure 4 and carries the same caption, so only Figure 4 is shown. Figure 8 is left off because Figure 9 shows the same tester.
Young's Modulus values on p.13 extract as 107. The page shows ten to the seventh power, and the lesson writes them out in a list, not as quotes.
The stress and carbon steel elongation checks use new numbers with the handbook's equations.
